topic: Compile-Time Polymorphism via Template Metaprogramming and its impact on Memory Layout and Performance
explanation: This explores how template metaprogramming enables compile-time polymorphism, contrasting it with runtime polymorphism achieved through virtual functions. We'll examine how compilers generate code for both, analyzing memory layout differences (virtual function tables vs. code generation per template instantiation), performance implications (runtime overhead of virtual function calls vs. compile-time optimization potential of templates), and potential pitfalls like code bloat from excessive template instantiations.  The focus will be on how the compiler handles the different mechanisms, potentially showing assembly-level differences.
syntax: C++ templates, template specialization, static polymorphism, CRTP (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern)
code_example: virtual void draw() = 0; // Pure virtual function for runtime polymorphism
void draw() override { std::cout << "Drawing Circle (Runtime Polymorphism)\n"; }
template <> struct StaticCircle<int> {void draw() { std::cout << "Drawing int Circle (Compile-Time Polymorphism)\n";}}
StaticCircle<double> circle_compile; // Compile time polymorphism via template instantiation
StaticCircle<int> intCircle; // Compile-time polymorphism with specialization
example_explanation: The example demonstrates runtime polymorphism using virtual functions and compile-time polymorphism using templates. The runtime version involves a virtual function table (vtable) adding runtime overhead. The compiler generates a separate function for each template instantiation in the compile-time version.  Examining the assembly output (using tools like gdb or objdump) would reveal the vtable's presence in the runtime version and the lack thereof in the compile-time version.  Excessive template instantiation can lead to code bloat, whereas the runtime approach has an inherent overhead per call. The example highlights potential performance trade-offs and the impact on memory layout due to the different implementation strategies.  The specialized `StaticCircle<int>` demonstrates how further customization happens at compile time without runtime overhead.
